Never assume one failed medication means all treatment will fail. Different drugs can have radically different outcomes in the same person. If the fit is poor, that may be a reason to keep investigating — not to give up.

ADHD medications do not “create discipline.” They change the operating conditions of brain networks involved in attention, initiation, reward, task persistence, arousal, emotional regulation and, in some people, motor timing or physical tension.
Two people can share an ADHD diagnosis while having very different dominant bottlenecks: one may mainly struggle with
, another with a mixture of all three. That is why the same medicine can feel transformative for one person and poor for another.

Amphetamine acts as a substrate at monoamine transporters and can alter intracellular monoamine handling and support transporter-mediated efflux. Experimental work also identifies intracellular TAAR1 signalling and transporter trafficking. Vesicular stores affect availability, but knockout-culture evidence shows vesicular transport is not an absolute prerequisite for every experimental amphetamine action. Calcium-triggered exocytosis is therefore kept separate from efflux. Models, concentration and exposure conditions limit translation. The UK dexamfetamine SmPC does not claim a fully settled explanation of behavioural benefit in ADHD. No dose, efficacy, safety or individual mechanism is inferred.

Supplements are not a substitute for appropriate medical treatment where treatment is indicated. Evidence quality varies widely.
ADHD treatment can alter the course of a person’s life for better or worse. Do
assume every service will protect you simply because it says it exists to help.
Keep copies of prescriptions, refusals, delays and outcome statements.
Document deterioration, side effects and functional impact.

Different medications can produce radically different outcomes. If a treatment is clearly wrong for you, do not assume that means all treatment will be wrong. Do not settle too early if the result is poor.
Blind trust is dangerous. Administrative pressure, delay or cost considerations may not align with your personal health needs. Protect yourself, keep records, and take treatment decisions seriously.
